lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A media company is deploying a news website for a worldwide audience. The website uses Amazon CloudFront as its content delivery network. Its backend runs on Amazon EC2 Windows instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The instances belong to an Auto Scaling group. The company’s customers access the website by using service example com as the CloudFront custom domain name. The CloudFront origin targets an ALB that uses service-alb.example.com as its domain name.  
  
The company’s security policy requires traffic to remain encrypted in transit at all times between users and the backend.  
  
Which combination of changes must the company make to satisfy this security requirement? (Choose three.)

options.text: Create a self-signed certificate for service.example.com. Import the certificate into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Configure CloudFront to use this imported SSL/TLS certificate. Change the default behavior to redirect HTTP to HTTPS.

Create a certificate for service.example.com by using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Configure CloudFront to use this custom SSL/TLS certificate. Change the default behavior to redirect HTTP to HTTPS.

Create a certificate with any domain name by using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for the EC2 instances. Configure the backend to use this certificate for its HTTPS listener. Specify the instance target type during the creation of a new target group that uses the HTTPS protocol for its targets. Attach the existing Auto Scaling group to this new target group.

Create a public certificate from a third-party certificate provider with any domain name for the EC2 instances. Configure the backend to use this certificate for its HTTPS listener. Specify the instance target type during the creation of a new target group that uses the HTTPS protocol for its targets. Attach the existing Auto Scaling group to this new target group.

Create a certificate for service-alb.example.com by using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). On the ALB add a new HTTPS listener that uses the new target group and the service-alb.example.com ACM certificate. Modify the CloudFront origin to use the HTTPS protocol only. Delete the HTTP listener on the ALB.

Create a self-signed certificate for service-alb.example.com. Import the certificate into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). On the ALB add a new HTTPS listener that uses the new target group and the imported service-alb.example.com ACM certificate. Modify the CloudFront origin to use the HTTPS protocol only. Delete the HTTP listener on the ALB.

questions.explanation:
A trusted certificate that covers `service.example.com` and a viewer policy that redirects HTTP to HTTPS encrypt the viewer-to-CloudFront connection. CloudFront must use HTTPS only to reach the ALB, whose HTTPS listener needs a trusted certificate covering `service-alb.example.com`; CloudFront requires the origin certificate to match the configured origin domain and rejects self-signed origin certificates. An HTTPS target group encrypts ALB-to-instance traffic, using certificates installed on the EC2 web servers; the ALB does not validate those target certificates.

**Learn more:** [Requirements for using SSL/TLS certificates with CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cnames-and-https-requirements.html) · [Origin settings for CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html)

A company operates an on-premises data center in the United States. The data center connects to AWS through an AWS Direct Connect connection. It has a private VIF connected to a Direct Connect gateway.  
  
Recently, the company opened a new data center in Europe and set up a new Direct Connect connection between the Europe data center and AWS. A new private VIF is connected to the existing Direct Connect gateway.  
  
The company wants to use Direct Connect SiteLink to establish a private network between the data center in the United States and the data center in Europe.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements in the **MOST** operationally efficient manner?

options.text: Create a new public VIF from each data center. Enable SiteLink on the new public VIFs.
Create a new transit VIF from each data center. Enable SiteLink on the new transit VIFs.
Use the existing VIF from each data center. Enable SiteLink on the existing private VIFs.
Create a new AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the data centers. Configure the new connection to use SiteLink.

questions.explanation:
Direct Connect SiteLink supports private virtual interfaces attached to a Direct Connect gateway and provides direct connectivity between Direct Connect points of presence over the AWS global network. Enabling SiteLink on the two existing private VIFs attached to the common Direct Connect gateway establishes the required private connectivity with no additional VIFs or VPN infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Direct Connect virtual interfaces and hosted virtual interfaces](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/WorkingWithVirtualInterfaces.html) · [Create a private virtual interface to the Direct Connect gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/create-private-vif-for-gateway.html)

A company has been using an obsolete application-layer protocol for communication between applications. The company has decided to stop using this protocol and must migrate every application to support a new protocol. Both the old and new protocols are TCP-based, but they use different port numbers.  
  
After several months of work, the company has migrated dozens of applications that run on Amazon EC2 instances and in containers. The company believes that every application has been migrated, but wants to validate that belief. A network engineer must verify that no application is still using the old protocol.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements without causing downtime?

options.text: Use Amazon Inspector and its Network Reachability rules package. Wait until the analysis has finished running to find out which EC2 instances are still listening to the old port.

Enable Amazon GuardDuty. Use the graphical visualizations to filter for traffic that uses the port of the old protocol. Exclude all internet traffic to filter out occasions when the same port is used as an ephemeral port.
Configure VPC flow logs to be delivered into an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the data and to filter for the port number that is used by the old protocol.

Inspect all security groups that are assigned to the EC2 instances that host the applications. Remove the port of the old protocol if that port is in the list of allowed ports. Verify that the applications are operating properly after the port is removed from the security groups.

questions.explanation:
Amazon VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic to and from VPC network interfaces and include source port, destination port, and protocol information. Flow logs delivered to Amazon S3 can be queried with Amazon Athena for TCP flows using the old protocol’s port, providing traffic-based verification without changing application connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Query Amazon VPC flow logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/vpc-flow-logs.html) · [Flow log records](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-log-records.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An international company plans to implement a multi-site hybrid infrastructure. The company intends to deploy cloud computing resources on AWS in the `us-east-1` Region and the `eu-west-2` Region, and in on-premises data centers in the United States (US) and the United Kingdom (UK). The data centers are connected to each other through a private WAN connection. IP routing information is exchanged dynamically by using BGP. The company wants two AWS Direct Connect connections, one in the US and one in the UK.  
  
The company expects to have 15 VPCs in each Region, with CIDR blocks that do not overlap with one another or with CIDR blocks in the on-premises environment. The VPC CIDR blocks are planned so prefix aggregation can occur both at a Regional level and across the entire AWS environment. The company will deploy a transit gateway in each Region to connect the VPCs. A network engineer plans to use a Direct Connect gateway in each Region. A transit VIF will connect the Direct Connect gateway in each Region to the transit gateway in that Region. The transit gateways will be peered with each other.  
  
The network engineer needs to ensure that traffic takes the shortest geographical path from source to destination. Traffic between the on-premises data centers and AWS must traverse a local Direct Connect connection. Traffic between the US data center and `eu-west-2`, and between the UK data center and `us-east-1`, must use the private WAN connection to reach the Direct Connect connection for the appropriate Region when that Direct Connect connection is available. The network must be resilient to failures of either the private WAN connection or the Direct Connect connections. The network must also reroute traffic automatically upon any failure.  
  
How should the network engineer configure the transit VIF associations on the Direct Connect gateways to meet these requirements?

options.text: Advertise only the aggregate route for the company's entire AWS environment.
Advertise VPC-specific CIDR prefixes from only the local Region. Additionally, advertise the aggregate route for the company’s entire AWS environment.
Advertise all the specific VPC CIDR blocks from both Regions.
Advertise both Regional aggregate prefixes. Configure custom BGP communities on the routes advertised toward the data center.

questions.explanation:
Advertising VPC-specific CIDR prefixes only from the local Region makes those routes the longest-prefix matches at the local data center, so local workloads use the local Direct Connect connection. The remote Region’s specific prefixes are learned through the private WAN from the other data center, which directs cross-Region traffic to the Direct Connect connection local to the destination Region. The aggregate prefix for the entire AWS environment is less specific and provides a BGP-reconvergent fallback through the remaining Direct Connect and inter-Region transit gateway path if the WAN or a Direct Connect connection fails. AWS Direct Connect evaluates the longest prefix first for private and transit VIF routing, and allowed prefixes from a Direct Connect gateway association are advertised to the on-premises network.

**Learn more:** [AWS Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html) · [Direct Connect gateways and Transit Gateway associations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-transit-gateways.html)

A company has two data centers interconnected by multiple redundant links from different suppliers. The company uses IP addresses in the `172.16.0.0/16` CIDR block. It runs iBGP between the two data centers using a private Autonomous System Number (ASN) and an IGP.  
  
The company is moving to a hybrid configuration in which it will initially use one VPC in the AWS Cloud. An AWS Direct Connect connection runs from the first data center to a Direct Connect gateway through a private VIF. Over this connection, the company advertises a summarized route for the `172.16.0.0/16` network. The company plans to establish a second summarized route from the second data center to a different Direct Connect location.  
  
The company must implement a solution that routes traffic to and from AWS through the first Direct Connect connection. The second Direct Connect connection must be used only for failover.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Prepend the private ASN on the BGP announcements to AWS from the second data center. Add a second VIF in the first Direct Connect connection. Advertise the same network without any prepends from the first data center. Implement the same setup for the BGP announcement from AWS to the two data centers.

Tag the BGP announcements with the local preference BGP community tags. Set the tag to high preference for the first data center. Set the tag to low preference for the second data center.Configure the second data center’s router to have a lower local preference for the direct AWS BGP advertisements than for the advertisement from the fist data center.

Configure the Direct Connect gateway to prefer routing through the Direct Connect connection with the first data center. Configure the second data center’s router to have a lower local preference for the direct AWS BGP advertisements than for the advertisement from the first data center.
Configure the focal AWS Region BGP community tag on the BGP route that is advertised from the fist data center. Configure AS_PATH prepends on the BGP announcements from the second data center.

questions.explanation:
For private and transit virtual interfaces, AWS Direct Connect supports local-preference BGP community tags to implement active/passive routing when the advertised prefixes are the same. A higher local-preference community on the first connection makes AWS return traffic through that primary path, while a lower community on the second makes it the backup. Setting the second data center’s BGP local preference lower for directly learned AWS routes than for routes learned from the first data center makes its outbound AWS traffic traverse the first data center’s Direct Connect connection until the primary path fails.

**Learn more:** [Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)

A network engineer is designing a DNS architecture for a new AWS environment. The environment must resolve DNS names for endpoints on premises, and on-premises systems must resolve the names of AWS endpoints. The DNS architecture must allow individual accounts to manage subdomains.  
  
The network engineer must create one set of rules that works across multiple accounts to control this behavior. Additionally, the network engineer must use AWS native services whenever possible.  
  
Which combination of steps should the network engineer take to satisfy these requirements? (Choose three.)

options.text: Create an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone for the overall cloud domain. Plan to create subdomains that align to other AWS accounts that are associated with the central Route 53 private hosted zone.

Create AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory server endpoints in the central AWS account that hosts the private hosted zone for the overall cloud domain. Create a conditional forwarding rule in Microsoft Active Directory DNS to forward traffic to a DNS resolver endpoint on premises. Create another rule to forward traffic between subdomains to the VPC resolver.

Create Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints in the central AWS account that hosts the private hosted zone for the overall cloud domain. Create a forwarding rule to forward traffic to a DNS resolver endpoint on premises. Create another rule to forward traffic between subdomains to the Resolver inbound endpoint.
Ensure that networking exists between the other accounts and the central account so that traffic can reach the AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory DNS endpoints.
Ensure that networking exists between the other accounts and the central account so that traffic can reach the Amazon Route 53 Resolver endpoints.

Share the Amazon Route 53 Resolver rules between accounts by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Ensure that networking exists between the other accounts and the central account so that traffic can reach the Route 53 Resolver endpoints.

questions.explanation:
Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints and forwarding rules forward VPC DNS queries for on-premises domains to on-premises DNS resolvers. Resolver inbound endpoints accept DNS queries from on-premises resolvers for AWS private DNS names. A central Route 53 private hosted zone can provide the parent cloud domain while account-aligned subdomains support separate ownership. Sharing the Resolver rules through AWS RAM allows other accounts to associate the common rules with their VPCs; connectivity to the central Resolver endpoints is required. AWS Directory Service is not needed for this hybrid DNS design.

**Learn more:** [Considerations when creating inbound and outbound endpoints - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-choose-vpc.html) · [Managing forwarding rules - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-rules-managing.html)

A company has deployed an application where the application front end communicates with backend instances through a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in the same VPC. The application is highly available in two Availability Zones. The company needs to minimize the traffic that crosses Availability Zones. Traffic from the application front end must remain in the same Availability Zone unless no healthy target exists in that Availability Zone behind the NLB. If no healthy target exists in the same Availability Zone, traffic must be routed to the other Availability Zone.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a private hosted zone with weighted routing for each Availability Zone. Point the primary record to the local Availability Zone NLB DNS record. Point the secondary record to the Regional NLB DNS record. Configure the front end of the application to perform DNS lookups on the local private hosted zone records.
Turn off cross-zone load balancing on the NLConfigure the front end of the application to perform DNS lookups on the local Availability Zone NLB DNS record.

Create a private hosted zone. Create a failover record for each Availability Zone. For each failover record, point the primary record to the local Availability Zone NLB DNS record and point the secondary record to the Regional NLB DNS record. Configure the front end of the application to perform DNS lookups on the local private hosted zone records.
Enable sticky sessions (session affinity) so that the NLB can bind a user’s session to targets in the same Availability Zone.

questions.explanation:
Disabling NLB cross-zone load balancing confines each load balancer node to healthy targets in its own Availability Zone. Resolving the local Availability Zone NLB DNS record keeps front-end traffic local during normal operation. When that zone has no healthy targets, the NLB removes the corresponding zonal IP address from DNS, so new connections can be directed to a healthy Availability Zone.

A company operates stateful security appliances across multiple Availability Zones in a centralized shared services VPC. The AWS environment contains a transit gateway attached to application VPCs and to the shared services VPC. The application VPCs contain workloads deployed in private subnets across multiple Availability Zones. The stateful appliances in the shared services VPC inspect all east-west (VPC-to-VPC) traffic.  
  
Users report that inter-VPC traffic to different Availability Zones is being dropped. A network engineer confirmed this by sending Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) pings between workloads in different Availability Zones across the application VPCs. The network engineer has excluded security groups, stateful-device configurations, and network ACLs as causes of the dropped traffic.  
  
What is causing the traffic to be dropped?

options.text: The stateful appliances and the transit gateway attachments are deployed in a separate subnet in the shared services VPC.
Appliance mode is not enabled on the transit gateway attachment to the shared services VPC.
The stateful appliances and the transit gateway attachments are deployed in the same subnet in the shared services VPC.
Appliance mode is not enabled on the transit gateway attachment to the application VPCs.

questions.explanation:
Appliance mode must be enabled on the transit gateway attachment for the VPC that hosts the stateful appliances. It maintains Availability Zone and network-interface affinity for the lifetime of a flow, ensuring that forward and return traffic traverse the same appliance. Without it, inter-VPC traffic between different Availability Zones can be routed asymmetrically through different appliances, so the return packet is dropped because that appliance has no matching flow state.

**Learn more:** [How AWS Transit Gateway works – Stateful appliances and appliance mode](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html) · [AWS Transit Gateway traffic flow and asymmetric routing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/inline-traffic-inspection-third-party-appliances/transit-gateway-asymmetric-routing.html)

A company runs infrastructure services in multiple VPCs across multiple accounts in the `us-west-2` Region. The VPC CIDR blocks are non-overlapping. The company needs to connect the VPCs to its data centers by using AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnels.  
  
The connections must be encrypted in transit. In addition, each data center’s connection must route to the nearest AWS edge location. The connections must be highly available and support automatic failover.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy a transit gateway. Share the transit gateway with each of the other accounts by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Create VPC attachments to the transit gateway from each service account. Add routes to the on-premises subnet in each of the service VPC route tables by using the attachment as the gateway. Create Site-to-Site VPN tunnel attachments with dynamic routing to the transit gateway. Enable the acceleration feature for the Site-to-Site VPN connection. Configure the VPN tunnels on the on-premises equipment. Configure BGP peering.

Deploy VPN gateways to each account. Enable the acceleration feature for VPN gateways on each account. Add routes to the on-premises subnet in each of the service VPC route tables. Use the VPNs as the gateway. Configure the VPN tunnels on the on-premises equipment. Configure BGP peering.

Deploy a transit gateway. Share the transit gateway with each of the other accounts by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Create VPC attachments to the transit gateway from each service account. Add routes to the on-premises subnet in each of the service VPC route tables by using the attachment as the gateway. Create Site-to-Site VPN tunnel attachments with dynamic routing to the transit gateway. Enable the acceleration feature for the Site-to-Site VPN connection. Configure the VPN tunnels on the on-premises equipment. Configure static routing.

Deploy VPN gateways to each account. Enable the acceleration feature for VPN gateways on each account. Add routes to the on-premises subnet in each of the service VPC route tables. Use the VPNs as the gateway. Configure the VPN tunnels on the on-premises equipment. Configure static routing.

questions.explanation:
An accelerated AWS Site-to-Site VPN uses AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic from the on-premises network through the AWS edge location nearest the customer gateway device. Acceleration is supported only for Site-to-Site VPN connections attached to a Transit Gateway, not virtual private gateways. A Transit Gateway shared through AWS RAM provides centralized connectivity for VPCs in other accounts, while IPsec VPN tunnels encrypt traffic. Dynamic routing with BGP enables routing exchange and supports automated failover over the redundant VPN tunnels.

**Learn more:** [Accelerated AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/accelerated-vpn.html) · [AWS Transit Gateway + AWS Site-to-Site VPN](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-vpc-connectivity-options/aws-transit-gateway-vpn.html)

A media company plans to host an event that it will live stream to users. The company wants to use Amazon CloudFront.  
  
A network engineer creates a primary origin and a secondary origin for CloudFront. The engineer must ensure that the primary origin can fail over to the secondary origin within 15 seconds if a disruption occurs.  
  
Which solution meets this requirement with the **LEAST** operational overhead?

options.text: Configure a Lambda@Edge function to check the health status of both origins every 10 seconds. Reroute incoming requests when the origin health status is unhealthy.
Create a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of both origins Configure the NLB as the origin in CloudFront.
Set the CloudFront origin connection timeout value to 5 seconds Set the origin connection attempts value to 2.
Configure a Lambda@Edge function to monitor incoming requests for an origin response. Reroute incoming requests if no response is received from the primary origin within 10 seconds.

questions.explanation:
For a CloudFront origin group, the origin connection timeout and connection-attempt settings determine how long CloudFront tries the primary origin before attempting the secondary origin. A 5-second connection timeout with two attempts results in up to 10 seconds before failover, meeting the 15-second requirement through managed CloudFront configuration rather than custom Lambda@Edge logic.

**Learn more:** [Optimize high availability with CloudFront origin failover](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/high_availability_origin_failover.html) · [Origin settings - Amazon CloudFront](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs multiple workloads in one VPC with public and private subnets. The company sets up an AWS Direct Connect connection to provide connectivity between its on-premises network and the VPC.  
  
The company buys a domain in its AWS account. Requests originating from the company’s network must resolve the domain to a private Application Load Balancer (ALB). Requests originating from the internet must resolve the domain to a public ALB.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the domain. Create an AWS Lambda@Edge function that inspects each request and routes requests from the internet to the public ALB. Configure the Lambda@Edge function to route requests from the company’s network to the private ALB. Create an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain. Include an A record that is configured as an alias that points to the CloudFront distribution.

Create an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain. Include an alias record that points to the public ALCreate a Route 53 private hosted zone for the domain. Include an alias record that points to the private ALConfigure a Route 53 inbound resolver endpoint on the VPC. Configure the company's network DNS to forward queries for the domain to the endpoint.

Create an Amazon Route 53 public hosted zone for the domain. Include an alias record that points to the public ALB. Create an additional alias record for the domain that routes to the private ALB. Associate a geolocation routing policy with the CIDR range of the company’s network.

Deploy new Amazon EC2 instances that host DNS servers in each of the private subnets. Configure the DNS servers to return the IP address of the public ALB for requests from the internet. Configure the DNS servers to return the IP address of the private ALB for requests from the company’s network. Configure a public Amazon Route 53 inbound resolver to forward all requests for the domain to the EC2 instances. Enable client IP preservation.

questions.explanation:
A Route 53 public hosted zone can provide the public alias record for internet DNS resolution, while a private hosted zone associated with the VPC can provide an alias record with the same name for the private ALB. Configuring the on-premises DNS resolver to forward queries for that domain to a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint allows clients on the company network, connected through Direct Connect, to resolve the private hosted-zone record. Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints accept DNS queries from an on-premises network, and private hosted zones are resolvable through an inbound endpoint connected to an associated VPC.

**Learn more:** [Forwarding inbound DNS queries to your VPCs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-forwarding-inbound-queries.html) · [Working with private hosted zones](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/hosted-zones-private.html)

A company uses a 1 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection to link its AWS environment with its on-premises data center. The connection gives employees access to an application VPC hosted on AWS. Many remote employees use a company-provided VPN to connect to the data center. These employees report slowness when accessing the application during business hours. On-premises users have begun reporting similar slowness while working in the office.  
  
The company plans to build an additional application on AWS. Both on-site and remote employees will use the additional application. After this application is deployed, the company will require 20% more bandwidth than it currently uses. With the increased usage, the company wants to add resiliency to its AWS connectivity. A network engineer must review the current implementation and make improvements within a limited budget.  
  
What should the network engineer do to meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Set up a new 1 Gbps Direct Connect dedicated connection to accommodate the additional traffic load from remote employees and the additional application. Create a link aggregation group (LAG).
Deploy an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to the application VPC. Configure the on-premises routing for the remote employees to connect to the Site-to-Site VPN connection.
Deploy Amazon Workspaces into the application VPInstruct the remote employees to connect to Workspaces.

Replace the existing 1 Gbps Direct Connect connection with two new 2 Gbps Direct Connect hosted connections. Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint in the application VPC. Instruct the remote employees to connect to the Client VPN endpoint.

questions.explanation: A second 1 Gbps dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection in a link aggregation group provides up to 2 Gbps of aggregate capacity and improves resiliency through multiple physical connections. It accommodates the additional bandwidth requirement while avoiding the unnecessary cost of two 2 Gbps hosted connections.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses transit gateways to route traffic among the company's VPCs. Each transit gateway has one route table. Each route table includes attachments and routes for VPCs in the same AWS Region as that transit gateway. The route tables in every VPC also include routes to all other VPC CIDR ranges reachable through the transit gateways. Some VPCs route through local NAT gateways.  
  
The company plans to add many new VPCs soon. A network engineer needs a solution for adding new VPC CIDR ranges to the route tables in each VPC.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements in the **MOST** operationally efficient way?

options.text: Create a new customer-managed prefix list. Add all VPC CIDR ranges to the new prefix list. Update the route tables in each VPC to use the new prefix list ID as the destination and the appropriate transit gateway ID as the target.
Turn on default route table propagation for the transit gateway route tables. Turn on route propagation for each route table in each VPC.
Update the route tables in each VPC to use 0.0.0.010 as the destination and the appropriate transit gateway ID as the target.
Turn on default route table association for the transit gateway route tables. Turn on route propagation for each route table in each VPC.

questions.explanation:
A customer-managed prefix list groups the VPC CIDR ranges behind a single reusable destination. A VPC route can use that prefix list as its destination and the transit gateway as its target; updating the prefix list later adds or removes CIDR ranges without editing every VPC route table. This also avoids replacing the default route required by VPCs that send internet-bound traffic to local NAT gateways. AWS Transit Gateway propagation populates transit gateway route tables, not VPC route tables.

**Learn more:** [Optimize AWS infrastructure management with prefix lists](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/managed-prefix-lists-referencing.html) · [How AWS Transit Gateway works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A network engineer must configure an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to operate a Linux-based network appliance in a highly available architecture. The network engineer is configuring the new launch template for the Auto Scaling group.  
  
Besides the primary network interface, the network appliance needs a second network interface that the application will use exclusively to exchange traffic with hosts on the internet. The company has configured a Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP) pool that contains an Elastic IP address which must serve as the public IP address of the second network interface.  
  
How should the network engineer implement the required architecture?

options.text: Configure the two network interfaces in the launch template. Define the primary network interface to be created in one of the private subnets. For the second network interface, select one of the public subnets. Choose the BYOIP pool ID as the source of public IP addresses.

Configure the primary network interface in a private subnet in the launch template. Use the user data option to run a cloud-init script after boot to attach the second network interface from a subnet with auto-assign public IP addressing enabled.

Create an AWS Lambda function to run as a lifecycle hook of the Auto Scaling group when an instance is launching. In the Lambda function, assign a network interface to an AWS Global Accelerator endpoint.

During creation of the Auto Scaling group, select subnets for the primary network interface. Use the user data option to run a cloud-init script to allocate a second network interface and to associate an Elastic IP address from the BYOIP pool.

questions.explanation:
Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling ignores subnet settings for additional interfaces in a launch template and creates all launch-template network interfaces in the instance subnet selected by the Auto Scaling group. Auto-assigned public IPv4 addressing is limited to the primary interface, whereas an Elastic IP can be associated with a specific network interface. Creating and attaching the secondary interface after launch and associating the BYOIP Elastic IP to it satisfies both requirements.

The company recently launched two EC2 instances in the financial application VPC. These new EC2 instances must receive the multicast stock trading data from the EC2 instance in the stock trading VPC.

Request a hosted public VIF from the APN Partner.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company is migrating an application from on premises to AWS. The company will host the application on Amazon EC2 instances deployed in a single VPC. During the migration period, DNS queries from the EC2 instances must resolve the names of on-premises servers. The migration is expected to last 3 months. After that 3-month migration period, resolving on-premises servers will no longer be necessary.  
  
What should a network engineer do to meet these requirements with the **LEAST** configuration?

options.text: Set up an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between on premises and AWS. Deploy an Amazon Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the Region that is hosting the VPC.
Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection with a private VIF. Deploy an Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint and a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the Region that is hosting the VPC.
Set up an AWS Client VPN connection between on premises and AWS. Deploy an Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC.

Set up an AWS Direct Connect connection with a public VIF. Deploy an Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the Region that is hosting the VPC. Use the IP address that is assigned to the endpoint for connectivity to the on-premises DNS servers.

questions.explanation:
A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint conditionally forwards DNS queries originating in a VPC to DNS resolvers on a connected on-premises network. AWS Site-to-Site VPN supplies suitable temporary private connectivity and is simpler to provision for a three-month migration than Direct Connect. Inbound Resolver endpoints are for DNS queries that originate on-premises and need resolution in a VPC, which is the opposite traffic direction.

**Learn more:** [Forwarding outbound DNS queries to your network - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-forwarding-outbound-queries.html) · [Resolving DNS queries between VPCs and your network - Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-overview-DSN-queries-to-vpc.html)

A network engineer needs to establish network connectivity between the company's VPCs and the partner's VPCs in `us-east-1`.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements with **MINIMUM** changes to both networks?

options.text: Create a new VPC in a new account. Deploy a router from AWS Marketplace. Share TGW-C and TGW-P with the new account by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Associate TGW-C and TGW-P with the new VPC. Configure the router in the new VPC to route between TGW-C and TGW-P.

Each data center connects to its closest AWS Direct Connect facility. The company uses Direct Connect connections, transit VIFs, and a single Direct Connect gateway to establish connectivity from its data centers to VPCs in us-east-1 and us-east-2. The company also has private connectivity from a telecommunications provider that connects the first data center to the second data center.  
  
Recently, the private connectivity between the data centers has experienced multiple connection disruptions. The company needs a solution to improve the reliability of the connection between the two data centers.  
  
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a new Direct Connect gateway. Enable the Direct Connect SiteLink feature on the transit VIF. Share the CIDR blocks from the first data center and the second data center with each other.
Create a new public VIF to both Regions. Enable the Direct Connect SiteLink feature on the new public VIF.
Enable the Direct Connect SiteLink feature on the existing Direct Connect connections.
Enable the Direct Connect SiteLink feature on the existing transit VIFS that are attached to the existing Direct Connect gateway.

questions.explanation:
AWS Direct Connect SiteLink enables direct connectivity between Direct Connect points of presence using the AWS network, allowing on-premises sites to communicate without routing through an AWS Region. SiteLink is supported on transit VIFs and can be enabled on the existing transit VIFs attached to the shared Direct Connect gateway, providing a more reliable path between the data centers.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company uses an AWS Organizations organization to manage multiple AWS accounts. The company is centralizing VPC endpoint access in a shared services VPC in its networking AWS account. The network engineer wants to minimize the operational overhead for other teams of configuring DNS resolution in an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone when they add new centralized VPC endpoints. Which combination of actions meets these requirements with the **LEAST** operational overhead? (Choose two.)

In a CloudFormation stack set, create an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes an AWS Lambda function any time a user creates a new private hosted zone.
Create an AWS Lambda function that has cross-account permissions. Configure the Lambda function to associate a private hosted zone with each of the spoke VPCs.
Create the VPC endpoint, private hosted zone, and private hosted zone association to the Route 53 Profile resources in the same AWS CloudFormation stack in the networking AWS account.

questions.explanation:

A company is expanding rapidly. Data transfers between the company’s on-premises systems and Amazon EC2 instances running in VPCs are constrained by the throughput of a single AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the company’s on-premises data center firewall and an AWS Transit Gateway.  
  
A network engineer must address the throttling by designing a highly available and secure solution. The solution must also scale VPN throughput from on premises to the VPC resources to accommodate increased traffic.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure multiple dynamic BGP-based Site-to-Site VPN connections to the transit gateway. Configure equal-cost multi-path routing (ECMP).
Configure multiple static routing-based Site-to-Site VPN connections to the transit gateway. Configure equal-cost multi-path routing (ECMP).
Configure a new Site-to-Site VPN connection to the transit gateway. Enable acceleration for the Site-to-Site VPN connection.
Configure a software appliance-based VPN connection over the internet from the on-premises firewall to an EC2 instance that has a large instance size and networking capabilities.

questions.explanation:
AWS Transit Gateway supports equal-cost multipath (ECMP) routing to load-balance traffic and aggregate bandwidth across multiple Site-to-Site VPN tunnels. ECMP requires dynamically routed BGP VPN connections; it is unsupported for static-routing VPN connections. Multiple BGP-based VPN connections provide redundant encrypted paths and horizontally scale throughput.

**Learn more:** [AWS Transit Gateway quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/transit-gateway-quotas.html) · [AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Site-to-Site VPN](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-vpc-connectivity-options/aws-transit-gateway-vpn.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A banking company successfully runs its public mobile-banking stack on AWS. The mobile-banking stack is deployed in a VPC that contains private and public subnets. The company uses IPv4 networking and has neither deployed nor supported IPv6 in the environment. The company has decided to adopt a third-party service provider's API and must integrate that API with the existing environment. The service provider’s API requires IPv6.  
  
A network engineer must enable IPv6 connectivity for the existing workload deployed in a private subnet. The company does not want to allow IPv6 traffic from the public internet and requires the company's servers to initiate all IPv6 connectivity. The network engineer enables IPv6 in the VPC and the private subnets.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an internet gateway and a NAT gateway in the VPC. Add a route to the existing subnet route tables to point IPv6 traffic to the NAT gateway.
Create an internet gateway and a NAT instance in the VPC. Add a route to the existing subnet route tables to point IPv6 traffic to the NAT instance.
Create an egress-only Internet gateway in the VPAdd a route to the existing subnet route tables to point IPv6 traffic to the egress-only internet gateway.
Create an egress-only internet gateway in the VPC. Configure a security group that denies all inbound traffic. Associate the security group with the egress-only internet gateway.

questions.explanation:
An egress-only internet gateway provides outbound-only IPv6 internet connectivity for instances in a VPC and prevents hosts on the internet from initiating IPv6 connections to those instances. Adding a `::/0` route from the private subnet route table to the egress-only internet gateway permits workload-initiated API access and return traffic without public-initiated IPv6 access.

**Learn more:** [Enable outbound IPv6 traffic using an egress-only internet gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/egress-only-internet-gateway.html) · [Add IPv6 support for your VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-migrate-ipv6-add.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company’s network engineer creates and tests VPC network designs in a development account. The company must monitor changes made to network resources, ensure strict adherence to network security policies, and retain access to the historical configurations of network resources.  
  
Which solution satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) rule with a custom pattern to monitor the account for changes. Configure the rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function to identify noncompliant resources. Update an Amazon DynamoDB table with the changes that are identified.

Create custom metrics from Amazon CloudWatch logs. Use the metrics to invoke an AWS Lambda function to identify noncompliant resources. Update an Amazon DynamoDB table with the changes that are identified.
Record the current state of network resources by using AWS Config. Create rules that reflect the desired configuration settings. Set remediation for noncompliant resources.

Record the current state of network resources by using AWS Systems Manager Inventory. Use Systems Manager State Manager to enforce the desired configuration settings and to carry out remediation for noncompliant resources.

questions.explanation:
AWS Config records configuration changes and preserves historical resource configurations. AWS Config rules continuously evaluate recorded resources against required security configuration settings, and remediation actions can correct resources found to be noncompliant.

**Learn more:** [What Is AWS Config?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/WhatIsConfig.html) · [AWS Config terminology and concepts](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/config-concepts.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A global company is setting up network connectivity between its primary and secondary data centers and a VPC. A network engineer must maximize the resiliency and fault tolerance of the connections. The network bandwidth must exceed 10 Gbps.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Set up a 100 Gbps connection at the primary data center that terminates at an AWS Direct Connect location. Set up a second 100 Gbps connection at the secondary data center that terminates at a second Direct Connect location. Ensure the connections are managed by separate providers.

Set up a 10 Gbps connection at the primary data center that terminates at an AWS Direct Connect location. Set up a second 10 Gbps connection at the secondary data center that terminates at a second Direct Connect location. Ensure the connections are managed by separate providers.

Set up two 10 Gbps connections at the primary data center that terminate at one AWS Direct Connect location. Ensure the connections are managed by separate providers. Set up two 10 Gbps connections at the secondary data center that terminate at a second Direct Connect location. Ensure the connections are managed by separate providers.

Set up a 10 Gbps connection at the primary data center that terminates at an AWS Direct Connect location. Set up an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection at the secondary data center that terminates at a virtual private gateway in the same Region as the company’s VPC.

questions.explanation:
Two 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connections at each data center provide more than 10 Gbps of aggregate bandwidth while retaining redundant paths through separate providers. Placing the primary and secondary data centers at different Direct Connect locations provides resilience to device, connectivity, and location failures without the cost of 100 Gbps circuits. AWS defines maximum Direct Connect resiliency as separate connections terminating on separate devices in more than one on-premises and Direct Connect location.

**Learn more:** [AWS Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/resiliency_toolkit.html) · [AWS Well-Architected Framework: Provision redundant connectivity between private networks and AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/rel_planning_network_topology_ha_conn_private_networks.html)

A company wants to use SSL/TLS certificates issued by AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to protect its social media web application. The application runs on backend Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company uses Amazon Route 53 to manage its DNS records. The company must integrate ACM with the EC2 instances and Route 53.  
  
Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Request a public certificate from ACM for the domain name that is configured in Route 53. Configure the ALB to use the public certificate Configure the A record in Route 53 to point to the ALB alias.

Request a private certificate from ACM for the domain name that is configured in Route 53. Configure the ALB to use the private certificate. Configure the A record in Route 53 to point to the ALB domain name.

Request two private certificates from ACM for the domain name that is configured in Route 53. Configure the ALB to use one private certificate. Configure the A record in Route 53 to point to the ALB alias. Configure the backend EC2 instances to use the second private certificate.

Request a private certificate and a public certificate from ACM for the domain name that is configured in Route 53. Configure the ALB to use the public certificate. Configure the A record in Route 53 to point to the ALB domain name. Configure the backend EC2 instances to use the private certificate.

questions.explanation:
An ACM public certificate provides browser-trusted TLS for an internet-facing application and can be associated with an ALB HTTPS listener. The ALB can terminate TLS and forward requests to its backend EC2 instances, so a separate certificate on each instance is unnecessary. A Route 53 A alias record can route the application domain directly to the ALB.

**Learn more:** [AWS Certificate Manager integrations with other AWS services](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/acm-services.html) · [Routing traffic to an ELB load balancer with Amazon Route 53](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-to-elb-load-balancer.html)

A company has created three VPCs: a production VPC, a nonproduction VPC, and a shared services VPC. The production VPC and the nonproduction VPC must each be able to communicate with the shared services VPC. Communication between the production VPC and the nonproduction VPC must not be allowed. A transit gateway is deployed to enable communication among the VPCs.  
  
Which transit gateway route table configurations meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure a route table with the production and nonproduction VPC attachments associated with propagated routes for only the shared services VPC. Create an additional route table with only the shared services VPC attachment associated with propagated routes from the production and nonproduction VPCs.

Configure a route table with the production and nonproduction VPC attachments associated with propagated routes for each VPC. Create an additional route table with only the shared services VPC attachment associated with propagated routes from each VPC.

Configure a route table with all the VPC attachments associated with propagated routes for only the shared services VPCreate an additional route table with only the shared services VPC attachment associated with propagated routes from the production and nonproduction VPCs.

Configure a route table with the production and nonproduction VPC attachments associated with propagated routes disabled. Create an additional route table with only the shared services VPC attachment associated with propagated routes from the production and nonproduction VPCs.

questions.explanation:
Transit Gateway routes traffic according to the route table associated with the source attachment. A route table associated with the production and nonproduction attachments that contains only the shared-services route permits both VPCs to reach shared services while omitting routes between production and nonproduction. A separate route table associated with the shared-services attachment must contain propagated routes to both production and nonproduction to provide return connectivity. AWS documents this isolated-router pattern: isolated attachments have no routes to one another but can communicate with a shared-services attachment.

**Learn more:** [How AWS Transit Gateway works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html) · [Transit gateway route tables in AWS Transit Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-route-tables.html)

A company operates an application across multiple AWS Regions and multiple Availability Zones. The company must expand into a new AWS Region. Low latency is essential to the application’s functionality.  
  
A network engineer needs to collect latency metrics between the existing Regions and the new Region. The network engineer must collect metrics covering at least the prior 30 days.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure an AWS Network Access Analyzer Network Access Scope, and use the analysis to review the latency.
Set up AWS Network Manager Infrastructure Performance. Publish network performance metrics to Amazon CloudWatch.
Use an Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer path to review the latency.
Set up VPC Flow Logs. Publish log metrics to Amazon CloudWatch.

questions.explanation:
AWS Network Manager Infrastructure Performance supplies historical network-latency metrics between AWS Regions and supports a time range of up to 30 days. Its metrics can also be published to Amazon CloudWatch, making it suitable for reviewing latency between the existing and new Regions.

**Learn more:** [What is Infrastructure Performance for AWS Network Manager?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/network-manager/latest/infrastructure-performance/what-is-nmip.html) · [Amazon CloudWatch subscriptions for Infrastructure Performance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/network-manager/latest/infrastructure-performance/nmip-subscriptions-cw.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company plans to migrate to AWS and use multiple VPCs across multiple AWS Regions. A network engineer must connect the `eu-west-1` and `eu-central-1` Regions to the company headquarters and branch office, respectively.  
  
The network engineer created a production VPC named Prod A with the CIDR block `10.0.0.0/16`. Prod A runs in an account in `eu-west-1`. The network engineer then created another production VPC named Prod B with the CIDR block `10.1.0.0/16`. Prod В runs in a different account in `eu-central-1`.  
  
The network engineer took the following steps in an attempt to achieve the required connectivity:  
  
1. Created one transit gateway in each Region.  
2. Shared and accepted the transit gateways with the production accounts in both Regions.  
3. Configured the peering attachment between the two transit gateways.  
4. Attached both VPCs to the transit gateway in their respective Region.  
5. Created both transit gateway route tables and associated the attachments with those route tables.  
6. Configured a static route in both transit gateway route tables to send traffic to the remote VPC in the other Region.  
7. Activated route propagation on the VPC route tables in each Region.  
  
After the configuration, the network engineer attempted to connect from Prod A to Prod B, but the connection was unsuccessful.  
  
What should the network engineer do to achieve the required connectivity?

options.text: Modify the IP address of the peering attachment to a wider range.
Delete the static routes that were in the transit gateway route table to send traffic to the remote VPC and enable route propagation instead.
Create a new route destined to 10.0.0.0/8 in both production VPC route tables with the Region transit gateway as the target.
Modify the transit gateway route tables from the production accounts to propagate routes dynamically between the production VPCs.

questions.explanation:
Transit gateway peering attachments support static routing, so each transit gateway route table must retain a static route to the remote VPC CIDR through its peering attachment. The VPC subnet route tables also need routes that send remote VPC traffic to the local transit gateway. A `10.0.0.0/8` route to the regional transit gateway in both production VPC route tables covers the remote `10.0.0.0/16` and `10.1.0.0/16` networks, while each VPC's more-specific local `/16` route remains preferred for local traffic.

**Learn more:** [Transit gateways in AWS Transit Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-transit-gateways.html) · [Transit gateway peering attachments in AWS Transit Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-peering.html)

A company needs to analyze TCP traffic sent to the internet. The traffic originates from Amazon EC2 instances in the company’s VPC, and the EC2 instances establish connections through a NAT gateway. Required information includes the source and destination IP addresses, ports, and the first 8 bytes of the TCP-segment payload. The company must collect, store, and analyze every required data point.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Set up the EC2 instances as VPC traffic mirror sources. Deploy software on the traffic mirror target to forward the data to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Analyze the data by using CloudWatch Logs Insights.

Set up the NAT gateway as a VPC traffic mirror source. Deploy software on the traffic mirror target to forward the data to an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster. Analyze the data by using OpenSearch Dashboards.
Turn on VPC Flow Logs on the EC2 instances. Specify the default format and a log destination of Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Analyze the flow log data by using CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Turn on VPC Flow Logs on the EC2 instances. Specify a custom format and a log destination of Amazon S3. Analyze the flow log data by using Amazon Athena.

questions.explanation:
VPC Traffic Mirroring copies inbound and outbound traffic from network interfaces attached to EC2 instances to a monitoring target, where software can decode the mirrored packets and extract both TCP/IP headers and payload bytes. VPC Flow Logs record flow-level metadata rather than packet payload, so they cannot provide the first 8 bytes of TCP-segment payload. CloudWatch Logs can store the data emitted by the target software and CloudWatch Logs Insights can analyze it.

**Learn more:** [How Traffic Mirroring works - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/mirroring/traffic-mirroring-how-it-works.html) · [Flow log records - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-log-records.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has multiple application accounts that contain dual-stack VPCs. The company wants to deploy a centralized DNS solution that supports IPv6.  
  
A network engineer deploys a shared services VPC. The engineer configures network connectivity among the company’s application VPCs, the shared services VPC, and the company’s on-premises environment, supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic.  
  
The network engineer uses Amazon Route 53 to deploy a centralized DNS solution. The engineer must ensure that resources in the application VPCs can perform DNS queries against an on-premises DNS resolver.  
  
Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint in the shared services VPC within a dual-stack subnet. Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the resolver rules to the application accounts.

Create a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the shared services VPC within a subnet that supports only IPv6. Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the endpoint to the application accounts.
Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint within a dual-stack subnet in each application VPUse AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the resolver rules to the application accounts.

Create a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint within a subnet that supports only IPv4 in each application VPC. Use AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share the resolver rules to the shared services account.

questions.explanation:
A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint forwards DNS queries originating in VPCs to DNS resolvers on the connected on-premises network. A dual-stack endpoint supports both IPv4 and IPv6 resolution. A forwarding rule that uses this centralized outbound endpoint can be shared through AWS RAM and associated with application VPCs in other accounts; sharing the rule also shares its outbound endpoint. An inbound endpoint is for DNS queries originating from the network toward AWS VPC resources, so it does not meet this traffic direction.

**Learn more:** [Values that you specify when you create or edit outbound endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-forwarding-outbound-queries-endpoint-values.html) · [Considerations when creating inbound and outbound endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-choose-vpc.html)

A company is establishing an AWS Direct Connect connection between its on-premises data center and AWS. The company currently has one VPC in its AWS account. The on-premises data center uses the `172.16.0.0/16` CIDR block, and the VPC uses the `10.1.1.0/24` CIDR block. The company associates the Direct Connect connection with one private VIF.  
  
A network engineer is told that SSH communication from hosts in the company's on-premises data center to Amazon EC2 instances deployed in the company's VPC is failing. The network engineer investigates and determines that the VIF is up and that a BGP peering session has been properly established.  
  
Which steps should the engineer take to troubleshoot this issue? (Choose three.)

options.text: Ensure that the advertised route for the on-premises network is present in the VPC route tables. Ensure that the VPC's subnets are present in the route tables of the on-premises network equipment.
Ensure that BGP community tags announcements from the customer gateway router are configured properly.
Ensure that the customer gateway router accepts BGP community tags in the prefixes the router receives.
Ensure that the VPC network ACLs allow inbound and outbound traffic for the on-premises network prefix.
Ensure that the security groups for the EC2 instances allow inbound SSH communication from the on-premises network prefix.
Ensure that the security groups for the EC2 instances allow outbound SSH communication from the on-premises network prefix.

questions.explanation:
For a private VIF with an established BGP session, traffic still requires bidirectional routes between the on-premises prefix and VPC prefix. The VPC route table must contain the on-premises prefix with the virtual private gateway as its target, and the on-premises equipment must route the VPC subnet through Direct Connect. Network ACLs must allow the required inbound and outbound traffic because they are stateless. The EC2 security group must permit inbound SSH from `172.16.0.0/16`; security groups are stateful, so return traffic for that allowed inbound connection does not require a separate outbound SSH rule. AWS Direct Connect troubleshooting guidance specifically calls for validating VPC routes, security groups, and network ACLs for the on-premises prefix.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot routing issues - AWS Direct Connect](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/ts-routing.html) · [Control traffic to resources using security groups - Amazon VPC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-security-groups.html)

A company operates a hybrid environment that links an on-premises data center with the AWS Cloud. The hybrid environment uses a 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection. The Direct Connect connection has multiple private VIFs that terminate in multiple VPCs.  
  
To meet regulatory requirements, the company must encrypt all WAN traffic, irrespective of the underlying transport. The company needs to implement an encryption solution that does not affect its bandwidth capacity.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a public VIF. Configure a new AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to use the new public VIF.
Configure MAC security (MACsec) support on the port of the existing Direct Connect connection. Change the encryption mode to must_encrypt.
Configure a new Direct Connect connection that supports MAC security (MACSec) Associate the existing VIFs to the new Direct Connect connection.
Create a public VIF. Configure a new private IP VPN that uses the Direct Connect connection.

questions.explanation:
MACsec encrypts traffic at Layer 2 on supported 10 Gbps dedicated AWS Direct Connect connections, preserving the connection’s bandwidth capacity. The `must_encrypt` encryption mode requires MACsec for all traffic and prevents transmission if encryption cannot be established, satisfying the requirement that all WAN traffic be encrypted.

**Learn more:** [MAC Security in Direct Connect](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/MACsec.html)

A company’s AWS environment contains two VPCs. VPC A uses the CIDR block `192.168.0.0/16`. VPC B uses the CIDR block `10.0.0.0/16`. Each VPC is deployed in a different AWS Region. The company has remote users who work outside the company offices. Those users must connect to an application running in the VPCs.  
  
Internet traffic to and from the VPCs must be encrypted. A network engineer must configure connectivity between the remote users and the VPCs.  
  
Which combination of steps should the network engineer take to satisfy these requirements with the **LEAST** management overhead? (Choose three.)

options.text: Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between VPC A and VPC B.
Establish a VPC peering connection between VPC A and VPC B.
Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint in VPC A and VPC B Add an authorization rule to grant access to VPC A and VPC B.
Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint in VPC A Add an authorization rule to grant access to VPC A and VPC B.
Add a route to the AWS Client VPN endpoint’s route table to direct traffic to VPC B.
Add a route to the AWS Client VPN endpoint's route table to direct traffic to VPC A.

questions.explanation:
AWS Client VPN provides encrypted remote-user access. A VPC peering connection allows the Client VPN target VPC, VPC A, to reach the non-overlapping CIDR range in VPC B across Regions. The Client VPN endpoint automatically adds a local route for its associated VPC A; a manually added endpoint route is required for the peered VPC B. Authorization rules must grant clients access to each destination network, so access must be authorized for both VPC A and VPC B.

**Learn more:** [How AWS Client VPN works](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/how-it-works.html) · [AWS Client VPN routes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-routes.html)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company runs application servers both on premises and on Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC. The application servers retrieve data hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket over the public internet. The EC2 instances in the VPC use an AWS Site-to-Site VPN to connect to the on-premises application servers.  
  
New company regulations require that all traffic between the application servers and the S3 bucket remain private and not use public IP addresses.  
  
Which solution will satisfy these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Configure an S3 gateway endpoint Modify the route table with the appropriate route for the endpoint. Access the S3 bucket through the gateway endpoint from the EC2 instances.
Configure an S3 interface endpoint. Update the on-premises servers and EC2 instances to use the interface endpoint DNS name to access the S3 bucket.

Configure an S3 interface endpoint. Update the on-premises servers to use the interface endpoint DNS name to access the S3 bucket. Configure an S3 gateway endpoint. Modify the route table so that the EC2 instances use the gateway endpoint.

Configure an S3 gateway endpoint. Modify the route table with the appropriate route for the endpoint. Use an S3 bucket policy to restrict access to the gateway endpoint. Configure a proxy server fleet behind a Network Load Balancer in the VPC so that the on-premises servers can access the S3 bucket.

questions.explanation:
An S3 gateway endpoint privately routes traffic originating in the VPC to Amazon S3 at no additional charge, but it cannot be used by resources on the other side of a Site-to-Site VPN. An S3 interface endpoint provides private S3 access for on-premises applications through the VPN, but has endpoint charges. Using the interface endpoint only for on-premises servers and the gateway endpoint for EC2 instances keeps both paths private while minimizing interface-endpoint cost.

**Learn more:** [Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html) · [AWS PrivateLink for Amazon S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/privatelink-interface-endpoints.html)

A company runs its application servers on Amazon EC2 instances. The EC2 instances run in separate VPCs that connect through a transit gateway. The EC2 instances launch in a private subnet with a route to the transit gateway for internal and external connectivity. External connectivity is provided by a VPC with firewall devices that inspect packets entering and leaving through an internet gateway.  
  
A network engineer needs to help the company’s application team increase the payload size per packet delivered between the EC2 instances. All network connectivity must pass through the transit gateway.  
  
What should the network engineer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable jumbo frames on the transit gateway. Instruct the application team to set the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of the system’s network interfaces to 9001 bytes.
Instruct the application team to set the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of the VPC to 8500 bytes.
Instruct the application team to set up enhanced networking on the system by using the enhanced networking adapter. Set the maximum transmission unit (MTU) to 9001 bytes.
Instruct the application team to set the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of the system’s network interfaces to 8500 bytes.

questions.explanation:
AWS Transit Gateway supports an MTU of 8,500 bytes for traffic between VPC attachments. Setting each EC2 instance network interface to an MTU of 8,500 bytes enables the largest supported packet size on the required transit-gateway path; 9,001-byte frames exceed that path’s MTU. [AWS Transit Gateway quotas — Maximum transmission unit (MTU)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/transit-gateway-quotas.html)

**Learn more:** [AWS Transit Gateway quotas — Maximum transmission unit (MTU)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/transit-gateway-quotas.html) · [Network maximum transmission unit (MTU) for your EC2 instance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/network_mtu.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A company has an AWS account containing four VPCs in the `us-east-1` Region. The VPCs include one development VPC and three production VPCs that host various workloads.  
  
The company has extended its on-premises data center to AWS through AWS Direct Connect by using a Direct Connect gateway. The company now needs connectivity from on premises to its production VPCs and development VPC. The production VPCs may route traffic to one another. However, the development VPC must remain isolated from the production VPCs. No traffic can flow between the development VPC and the production VPCs.  
  
To prepare for this solution, a network engineer creates a transit gateway with one transit gateway route table. Default route table association and default route table propagation are disabled. The network engineer attaches the production VPCs, development VPC, and Direct Connect gateway to the transit gateway. In each VPC route table, the network engineer adds a route for `0.0.0.0/0` that uses the transit gateway as the next hop.  
  
Which combination of steps should the network engineer perform next to complete the solution? (Choose three.)

options.text: Associate the production VPC attachments with the existing transit gateway route table. Propagate the routes from these attachments.
Associate all the attachments with the existing transit gateway route table. Propagate the routes from these attachments.
Associate the Direct Connect gateway attachment with the existing transit gateway route table. Propagate the Direct Connect gateway attachment to this route table.
Change the security group inbound rules on the existing transit gateway network interfaces in the development VPC to allow connections to and from the on-premises CIDR range only.

Create a new transit gateway route table. Associate the new route table with the development VPC attachment. Propagate the Direct Connect gateway and development VPC attachment to the new route table.
Create a new transit gateway with default route table association and default route table propagation turned on. Attach the Direct Connect gateway and development VPC to the new transit gateway.

questions.explanation:
Because default association and propagation are disabled, routing must be built explicitly. Option A associates the production VPC attachments with the existing route table and propagates their routes, enabling production-to-production reachability. Option C associates the Direct Connect gateway attachment with that same route table and propagates it, giving on-premises reachability to the production VPCs. Option E creates a second route table associated only with the development VPC and propagates the Direct Connect gateway and development attachment into it, so development can reach on-premises but stays isolated from production. This is the standard transit gateway VRF-style isolation pattern, using separate route tables per environment. Option B associates everything to one table (breaking isolation), D misapplies security groups to the transit gateway, and F needlessly builds a second transit gateway.

**Learn more:** [How transit gateways work (route tables & isolation)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html) · [Transit gateway route tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-route-tables.html)

A European automotive manufacturer plans to migrate its customer-facing services and analytics platform from two on-premises data centers to the AWS Cloud. Its on-premises data centers are separated by 50 miles (80.4 km), and it must preserve that separation between its two cloud locations. The company also requires failover capability between the two cloud locations.  
  
The infrastructure team creates multiple accounts to separate workloads and responsibilities. The company deploys resources in the eu-west-3 Region and the eu-central-1 Region. It chooses an AWS Direct Connect Partner in each Region and requests two resilient 1 Gbps fiber connections from each provider.  
  
The network engineer must establish connectivity among all VPCs in the accounts and between the on-premises network and the AWS Cloud. The solution must provide access to all services in both Regions if network issues occur.  
  
Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a Direct Connect gateway. Create a private VIF on each of the Direct Connect connections. Attach the private VIFs to the Direct Connect gateway. Use equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing to aggregate the four connections across the two Regions. Attach the Direct Connect gateway directly to each VPC's virtual private gateway.

Create a Direct Connect gateway. Create a transit gateway. Attach the transit gateway to the Direct Connect gateway. Create a transit VIF on each of the Direct Connect connections. Attach the transit VIFs to the Direct Connect gateway. Use a link aggregation group (LAG) to aggregate the four connections across the two Regions. Attach the transit gateway directly to each VPC.

Create a Direct Connect gateway. Create a transit gateway in each Region. Attach the transit gateways to the Direct Connect gateway. Create a transit VIF on each of the Direct Connect connections. Attach the transit VIFs to the Direct Connect gateway. Peer the transit gateways. Attach the transit gateways in each Region to the VPCs in the same Region.

Create a Direct Connect gateway. Create a private VIF on each of the Direct Connect connections. Attach the private VIFs to the Direct Connect gateway. Use a link aggregation group (LAG) to aggregate the four connections across the two Regions. Create a transit gateway. Attach the transit gateway to the Direct Connect gateway. Attach the transit gateway directly to each VPC.

questions.explanation:
A Direct Connect gateway associated with transit gateways uses transit virtual interfaces to provide on-premises connectivity to the VPCs attached to those transit gateways. Transit Gateway is a Regional service, so a transit gateway is needed in each Region for the local VPC attachments. An inter-Region transit gateway peering attachment provides routing between those Regional transit gateways, enabling cross-Region service access and failover. A single LAG cannot span the two Direct Connect locations because all LAG member connections must terminate at the same Direct Connect endpoint.

**Learn more:** [Direct Connect gateways and Transit Gateway associations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-transit-gateways.html) · [Transit gateway peering attachments in AWS Transit Gateway](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-peering.html)
